of a dispute over the meaning of a statute that subjects providers of 
“telecommunications service [s]” to mandatory common-carrier regulation. 
47 U.S.C. § 153(44) (2000) (recodified at 47 U.S.C. § 153(51)). In the order 
under review, the Federal Communications Commission concluded that 
cable companies selfing broadband Internet service do not provide 
“telecommunications service [s]” and, hence, were exempt from mandatory 
common-carrier regulation under the Communications Act of 1934. In 
rejecting the Commission’s interpretation, the Ninth Circuit relied on one 
of its precedents holding that cable modem sezrvice was a 
“telecommunications service” and, thus, did not analyze the permissibility 
of the Commission’s construction under Chevron's deferential framework.
Brand X rejected the Ninth Circuit’s approach. According to Brand X, 
“[a] court’s prior judicial construction of a statute trumps an agency 
construction otherwise entitled to Chevron deference only if the prior court 
decision holds that its construction follows from the unambiguous terms of 
the statute and thus leaves no room for agency discretion.” Brand X 
explained that the Ninth Circuit’s prior case would have “held only that 
the best reading of [the relevant statute] was that cable modem service was 
a ‘telecommunications service,’ not that it was the only permissible reading 
of the statute.” Brand X thus contemplated that an agency’s permissible 
construction could displace the best construction of a statute under some 
circumstances. As Brand X explained: “Chevron teaches that a court’s 
opinion as to the best reading of an ambiguous statute an agency is charged 
with administering is not authoritative.” To the contrary, “the agency may, 
consistent with the court’s holding, choose a different construction [from 
the court], since the agency remains the authoritative interpreter (within 
the limits of reason) of such statutes.” See also United States v. Home 
Concrete & Supply, LLC, 132 S. Ct. 1836 (2012).
Third: A series of cases elaborated on what became known as the 
“major questions” exception to Chevron. For instance, in FDA v. Brown & 
Williamson Tobacco Corp., 529 U.S. 120, 159 (2000), the Court declared 
that, “[i]n extraordinary cases, .. . there may be reason to hesitate before 
concluding that Congress has intended such an implicit delegation” under 
Chevron. And inXrn^ v. Burwell, 57^6 U.S. 473 (2015), the Court confronted

a state” to include a federally established insurance exchange. The Court 
remarked that, although it “often appl[ied] the two-step framework 
announced in Chevron” when analyzing agency interpretation of statutes, 
this was one of those “extraordinary cases” where it was “unlikely that 
Congress would have delegated this decision to the IRS, which has no
